You are the specialist for the law of Region A (region). You assess a proposed data transfer against the instruments in your corpus: Region A Personal Information Regulation.

Other jurisdictions in this system: Region B. You cannot read their law. If a requirement of your law depends on what another jurisdiction's law says, add a peer_question naming that jurisdiction's registry code and set open_dependency on the requirement; the supervisor routes it. Ask only what the other law provides on a point your own requirement depends on; never ask another specialist to assess your requirement, or to assess or confirm another corpus's provisions.
Lower-level corpora you may delegate to: subregion_a1. Where your law leaves a matter to that law, delegate a specific question with the provisions that leave it open. The delegate also reports further requirements of its own law.

METHOD
1. Decide whether your law applies to any party or activity in the case, from its scope provisions.
2. Work through your table of contents and identify every requirement your law imposes that the facts engage, including definitions that change the analysis and cumulative conditions in other provisions.
3. Assess each requirement. Keep requirements for different actors or activities separate.
4. Delegate and raise peer questions where needed.
5. In coverage_note, say how you checked nothing engaged was missed and what remains limited.

RULES
- The laws in your corpora are the only law. Do not import rules from any real-world legal system; if your general knowledge suggests a rule the text does not contain, or contradicts the text, follow the text.
- Facts: refer to FACT PASSAGES by fact_id. Requester statements are claims; evidence summaries describe what each document says.
- Treat the stated facts and described arrangements as complete. If a requirement fails on them, mark it unmet "as described" and put the cure in required_actions. A supplied document that addresses a requirement establishes it; list elements it omits as confirmations, not as blockers.
- status: met | unmet | undetermined (a decisive fact, document or answer from other law is missing: say which in missing_facts, missing_evidence or open_dependency) | not_applicable.
- kind: gate if the transfer may not proceed until it is met; duty if it is an ongoing obligation that does not decide whether this transfer may proceed.
- routes: for each requirement with alternatives or exceptions in the law, list every plausible one with a status. Do not stop at the first route that works if it carries its own prerequisites; a route that fails does not close the others. Route statuses are defined in the schema; apply them literally. supported means in place now. available means it would work for the transfer as proposed once the parties make the changes in required_actions: these are the routes forward. ruled_out means the law excludes the transfer as proposed, with a reason from the text. unresolved is only for a missing fact, document or answer, never for something not yet done. The status must match your reasoning: if your reasoning says the law excludes the route, it is ruled_out; if it says a change would make it work, it is available.
- A requirement is an obligation the law imposes. Each alternative way to meet it (a recognition, a set of clauses, an exception, a derogation) is a route inside that requirement, never a requirement of its own: one route failing does not make an obligation unmet while another route remains.
- Report only requirements created by your own instruments. Where your law applies another corpus's law as well (lower-level law, or another jurisdiction's), do not create a requirement for that law and do not assess its provisions: its own specialist reports it. Use its answer in your reasoning, or name it in open_dependency.
- Cite only provisions you have read, by ID (e.g. "A-REG 1"). quote_id must be a passage ID you were shown from a cited provision.
- Passage IDs such as "A-REG 1#L5" label lines of text, not paragraphs. In reasoning and questions, refer to a provision's own numbering (its article or section, paragraph and point numbers), never to an #L line label.

Also assess any Region B Records Access Act provisions concerning production, non-disclosure, encryption, or review.

output.applicability_reasoning: The Region B instruments are relevant because the recipient is established in Region B and the proposed transfer will be stored and accessed there. However, the Health Records Act's operative duties are party-specific. The transferred material is a health record under Section 2 because it identifies an individual and relates to physical health and the provision of health care. Harrow is not a covered provider: it does not bill a Region B-licensed health insurer electronically and is not an insurer. It is not a service agent because it keeps the information in its own clinical record for its own care, rather than on behalf of a covered provider. It is also not a data host because it does not store records on behalf of another person. The Records Access Act is relevant only as a potential power applicable to a Region B computing provider; no facts show that Harrow provides storage, hosting or computing services as a business.

requirements.title: Transferred material is a health record
requirements.reasoning: The report, ECG summary and referral letter identify one adult patient and relate to physical health and the provision of health care. They therefore fall within the Section 2 definition of health record. This characterisation does not itself make Harrow a covered provider, service agent or data host.

requirements.title: Permitted use or disclosure by a covered provider
requirements.reasoning: Sections 4 to 8 apply only to covered providers and service agents. Harrow does not bill a health insurer and is not an insurer, so it is not a covered provider under Section 2. It is not a service agent because it maintains the information in its own clinical record for its own care, not on behalf of a covered provider. Accordingly, Section 4 does not impose a Region B restriction on Harrow's receipt, review or video consultation. If Section 4 did apply, treatment would be an express route without written authorisation, and the supplied written consent would also support the written-authorisation route for any other use or disclosure; those routes are therefore reported but do not alter the non-applicability conclusion.

routes.name: Treatment without written authorisation
routes.reasoning: This route is available only to a covered provider, and Harrow is not a covered provider on the supplied facts.

routes.name: Written authorisation for another use or disclosure
routes.reasoning: The patient supplied written consent, but this route is also a Section 4 route applicable only to a covered provider; it is not a route imposed on Harrow as described.

confirmations: The supplied consent specifically identifies the documents, recipient, purpose and risks, and is evidence of written authorisation if Section 4 were otherwise applicable.

requirements.title: Minimum necessary handling
requirements.reasoning: Section 6 applies to a covered provider or service agent. Harrow is neither on the supplied facts. Therefore Region B's minimum-necessary rule does not impose a requirement on this recipient. The material sent is limited to the named patient's genetic report, ECG summary and referral letter, with no other record or family details, but that factual limitation does not change the statutory scope.

requirements.title: Administrative, physical and technical safeguards
requirements.reasoning: Section 7 applies to covered providers and service agents. Harrow is neither: it is a private clinic that does not bill an insurer and holds the information for its own care, not on behalf of a covered provider. The encrypted referral portal is a positive security fact, but Section 7 does not impose its safeguard duty on Harrow on these facts.

requirements.title: Retention by a data host
requirements.reasoning: Section 9 applies to a person that stores health records in Region B on behalf of another person. Harrow stores the referral in its own clinical record for its own patient care and stores no records on behalf of anyone else. It is therefore not a data host under Section 2, and the seven-year data-host retention rule and its foreign-origin return alternative do not apply. Its stated own clinical retention schedule is not regulated by Section 9.

routes.name: Retain for seven years as a data host
routes.reasoning: The seven-year route applies only to a data host, and Harrow does not store records on behalf of another person.

routes.name: Return foreign-origin record and retain no copy
routes.reasoning: This is an exception within the data-host rule. Harrow is not a data host, and the proposed arrangement expressly contemplates retention in its own clinical record.

requirements.title: Compliance with a Records Access Act production order
requirements.reasoning: Section 3 authorises the Commissioner to order a computing provider to produce records for national security or serious-crime investigations. The facts describe Harrow as a specialist health-care clinic, not as a person providing storage, hosting or computing services in Region B. No production order exists or is proposed. Accordingly, no present production duty is engaged by this transfer.
confirmations: If Harrow separately provides storage, hosting or computing services, or if the Commissioner issues an order for a qualifying purpose, the Section 3 analysis would need to be revisited.

requirements.title: Non-disclosure of a production order
requirements.reasoning: Section 4 concerns a computing provider subject to an order under Section 3 and permits the order to prohibit informing customers or others. No Section 3 order is described, and Harrow is not shown to be a computing provider. The provision creates no current duty for this referral.

requirements.title: Encrypted records and unavailable keys
requirements.reasoning: Section 5 limits what a computing provider must do under a Section 3 production order; it does not impose a general encryption duty. No qualifying order or computing-provider role is shown. The encrypted upload is consequently not a current requirement under the Records Access Act.

requirements.title: Review or notification of a production order
requirements.reasoning: Section 6 removes any right of the person to whom records relate to be notified of or seek review of a Section 3 order. No Section 3 order is described, so this provision has no current application to the proposed referral.

output.applicability_reasoning: The transfer involves identified personal information, including health and genetic information, and is made available to a recipient in Region B. The sender is established in Subregion A1, so the processing is within the territorial scope of the Regulation even though part of the processing occurs in Region B. The encrypted upload and the recipient's clinical record constitute processing by automated means and/or processing forming part of filing systems. The personal and identified nature of the information excludes the material-scope exceptions.

requirements.title: Lawful ground for processing
requirements.reasoning: Processing is lawful if at least one Article 6 ground applies. The supplied facts establish that the patient gave a clear written consent specifically covering the named report, ECG summary and referral letter for the stated treatment-related second-opinion purpose. The treatment-related processing is also described as being carried out by registered practitioners. Consent therefore supplies a lawful ground for the sending clinic's processing, subject to the consent conditions and sensitive-information requirements assessed separately.

routes.name: Consent
routes.reasoning: The adult patient gave a clear written statement for the specific treatment-related referral and transfer purpose.

routes.name: Contract performance or pre-contract steps
routes.reasoning: The facts describe terms of care, but do not establish that sending the report to the Region B specialist is necessary for performance of a contract with the patient.

routes.name: Legal obligation
routes.reasoning: No Region A or Subregion A1 legal obligation requiring this processing is supplied.

routes.name: Vital interests
routes.reasoning: The patient is an adult who can consent; the facts do not show that the transfer is necessary to protect vital interests in circumstances requiring this route.

routes.name: Public function
routes.reasoning: The clinic is described as a private provider and no public function vested by law is supplied.

routes.name: Legitimate interests
routes.reasoning: Article 6(2) makes this route unavailable for sensitive information, and the data includes health and genetic information.

confirmations: Confirm that the consent record is retained and remains available for audit.
Confirm that any withdrawal of consent is handled for future processing; withdrawal does not itself invalidate processing already carried out.

requirements.title: Conditions for consent
requirements.reasoning: The evidence establishes a signed written statement, specific identification of the information, recipient and second-opinion purpose, and an explanation of the risks where no recognition or safeguards exist. It also records that consent may be withdrawn at any time. The patient is an adult, so the under-16 rule is not engaged.

routes.name: Consent by person aged 16 or older
routes.reasoning: The patient is stated to be an adult capable of consenting, and the consent is written, purpose-specific and withdrawable.

routes.name: Parental-responsibility consent for a person under 16
routes.reasoning: The patient is an adult and no parental-responsibility route is relevant.

routes.name: Applicable Subregion-law lower age
routes.reasoning: The patient is an adult, so no lower-age rule is needed.

requirements.title: Sensitive-information prohibition and exception
requirements.reasoning: The report, ECG summary and referral letter contain health information and genetic information, which are sensitive information under Article 4. Article 8 otherwise prohibits processing, but the proposed processing is necessary for medical diagnosis and treatment and is carried out by or under the responsibility of registered clinical geneticists. The Article 8(2)(c) healthcare route therefore applies, subject to the Subregion A1 conditions. The proposed purpose is treatment rather than insurance or employment, so the A1 genetic-information restriction on consent for insurance or employment does not apply.

routes.name: Explicit consent for specified purposes
routes.reasoning: The patient gave explicit, purpose-specific written consent. The facts do not indicate an insurance or employment purpose that would trigger the A1 restriction on consent for genetic information.

routes.name: Healthcare, diagnosis or treatment by or under responsibility of a professional subject to secrecy
routes.reasoning: The treatment purpose and registration of the sending practitioners are supplied, but whether Subregion A1 law provides the required legal basis, professional-secrecy obligation and any additional conditions must be answered by the Subregion A1 specialist.

routes.name: Vital interests where consent is impossible
routes.reasoning: The patient can consent, so the incapacity condition is not met.

routes.name: Public interest in public health
routes.reasoning: The facts describe individual treatment and do not establish an applicable public-health legal basis.

routes.name: Scientific research
routes.reasoning: The purpose is a clinical second opinion before treatment, not scientific research.

missing_evidence: Subregion A1 law confirming the healthcare legal basis, professional-secrecy obligation and any further health/genetic-information conditions
confirmations: Confirm that both the sending consultant and the Region B specialist are acting for the patient's clinical care and not for insurance or employment purposes.
requirements.open_dependency: Whether Subregion A1 law supplies the Article 8(2)(c) healthcare legal basis and professional-secrecy conditions, and whether it imposes any further conditions applicable to this processing.

requirements.title: Impact assessment
requirements.reasoning: Article 12 requires an assessment before processing where processing is likely to result in a high risk. The specific automatic example for sensitive information concerns more than 5,000 persons; this transfer concerns one adult. It is a one-off clinical referral, not systematic large-scale monitoring. The supplied facts also do not describe hosting or storage by an agent outside A1 or matching with insurer information, the further A1 listed categories identified in the applicable graph. On the facts provided, the transfer is not shown to be likely to result in high risk and no assessment is required for this referral.
confirmations: Confirm that no Authority-published A1 list captures this clinical referral independently of the listed hosting/storage or insurer-matching categories.
Confirm that the Region B clinic is receiving the information into its own clinical record and is not acting as an external agent or data host for the A1 clinic.

requirements.title: General outward-transfer requirement
requirements.reasoning: Making the information available to the Region B specialist by upload and allowing access from Region B is an outward transfer. Article 16 requires compliance with the Regulation and coverage by recognition, approved clauses or a specific-situation derogation. The recognition route does not cover this transfer because Region B recognition is limited to certified recipients and non-sensitive information; the recipient lacks certification and the information is sensitive. No approved clauses exist. The one-off transfer is nevertheless covered by the explicit-consent derogation: the adult patient specifically consented after being informed of the absence of recognition and safeguards, and the transfer is occasional rather than repetitive, structural or continuing. The A1 specialist must confirm whether its law makes the consent route unavailable for genetic information; the supplied A1 graph indicates that it does, so the supervisor should incorporate that answer before treating this route as finally available.

routes.name: Recognition for Region B or certified recipients
routes.reasoning: Annex II limits recognition to active Region B Trusted Recipient Scheme certification and to non-sensitive information. The recipient has no certification, and the transfer includes health and genetic information.

routes.name: Approved transfer clauses
routes.reasoning: No approved clauses have been executed, so this route is not supported now. It would work for the proposed transfer if the parties execute Commission-approved clauses and the exporter completes the required assessment of Region B law and practice, adopting supplementary measures where necessary and not relying on this route if effective measures cannot be adopted.

routes.name: Specific-situation derogation: explicit consent
routes.reasoning: The consent is explicit and specifically identifies the transfer, recipient and purpose; it records that the patient was informed of the absence of recognition and safeguards and the possible risks. The transfer is one-off. This route remains subject to the Subregion A1 genetic-information restriction identified in the graph and delegated below.

routes.name: Specific-situation derogation: contract performance
routes.reasoning: The facts do not establish that the outward transfer is necessary for performance of a contract between the patient and the custodian. The clinic's terms of care say nothing about referrals outside Region A.

routes.name: Specific-situation derogation: vital interests
routes.reasoning: The patient can consent, so the required incapacity condition is absent.

routes.name: Specific-situation derogation: important public interest
routes.reasoning: No important public interest recognised in Region A or Subregion A1 law is supplied; this is an individual clinical referral.

missing_facts: Whether Subregion A1 law prohibits reliance on consent for this outward transfer of genetic information
confirmations: If the consent route is unavailable under Subregion A1 law, execute approved transfer clauses before transferring and complete the Article 18 assessment and any necessary supplementary measures.
requirements.open_dependency: Whether Subregion A1 law makes the Article 19(1)(a) explicit-consent derogation unavailable for an outward transfer concerning genetic information.

requirements.title: Processing principles and accountability
requirements.reasoning: The stated processing has a specified treatment purpose, is limited to the report, ECG summary, identity details and referral letter needed for the second opinion, and excludes the rest of the record and family information. The one-off encrypted upload supplies an appropriate security measure on the facts. Each clinic retains the information in its own clinical record for the patient's care. The supplied facts support compliance with purpose limitation, data minimisation, retention limitation and security as an ongoing duty.
confirmations: Confirm accuracy and currency of the identifying and clinical information before sending.
Confirm that each retention schedule limits identifiable retention to what is necessary for the relevant care purpose.
Confirm that the portal access controls and encryption remain appropriate and that no onward transfer is made.

requirements.title: Accountability for compliance
requirements.reasoning: The clinic is the custodian responsible for demonstrating compliance with the processing principles. The supplied consent record and referral correspondence provide supporting compliance records, and the transfer method and retention arrangements are described.
confirmations: Retain documentation of the Article 16 route selected and the A1-law determination.

answers.answer: Yes. Subregion A1 law supplies the health-care processing basis: processing health information is lawful where it is necessary for health care or treatment and is carried out by or under the responsibility of a registered practitioner. Kestrel's consultant clinical geneticists are registered medical practitioners, and the second-opinion processing is for deciding the patient's treatment. A registered practitioner also owes professional secrecy concerning health information obtained in practice. Disclosure to Harrow is permitted on the patient-consent route, and the supplied signed consent specifically identifies the information, recipient, purpose and transfer risks. The agent exception is not relevant because Harrow is receiving and retaining the information for its own care, not acting only on Kestrel's documented instructions as an agent. The further A1 limitation is that the professional may disclose only with patient consent, where required by law, or to prevent a serious and imminent threat to life; consent satisfies that limitation here. No A1 requirement for an impact assessment or Section 6 hosting/storage notice is triggered by the facts described.

Yes, for the proposed genetic-information transfer. Section 7 expressly provides that genetic information may not be made the subject of an outward transfer on the basis of Article 19(1)(a). Accordingly, the patient's explicit consent cannot support the Article 19(1)(a) derogation for this transfer, even though the consent is otherwise specific and informed. Section 7's separate consent restriction for lifting the Article 8(1) prohibition applies only where genetic information is processed for insurance or employment purposes; this case is for treatment, so that separate restriction is not engaged. Section 7 does not itself exclude every other possible outward-transfer route under the Region A Regulation, but this consent-based route is unavailable under A1 law.

No additional Section 6 hosting/storage conditions are triggered on the described arrangement. Section 6 applies where a custodian established in A1 makes an outward transfer of patients' health records for hosting or storing them. Harrow is described as keeping the referral in its own clinical record for its own patient care, storing no records on behalf of anyone else. That is not the described hosting or storage of a patient record system by an agent, and the transfer is a one-off clinical referral rather than outsourcing Kestrel's record storage. Therefore A1's 30-day written Commission notice and A1-only decryption-key requirements do not apply under Section 6. The encrypted upload is consistent with secure handling, but it does not turn the arrangement into Section 6 hosting/storage. The general outward-transfer requirements in Articles 16 to 19 remain matters for the Region A specialist to assess; A1 law does not replace them. Separately, professional secrecy still requires a permitted disclosure, which is satisfied here by the patient's consent, subject to the genetic-transfer restriction reported above.

No. Section 8 requires an impact assessment regardless of the number of persons concerned only for two listed activities: hosting or storage of a patient record system by an agent outside A1, or matching health information with information held by an insurer. The facts describe neither. Harrow is not acting as an agent hosting Kestrel's patient record system; it keeps the referral in its own clinical record for its own care. There is also no insurer, insurer billing, or insurer matching. The one-person, one-off nature of the referral therefore does not independently trigger an A1 impact assessment under Section 8.

confirmations: Articles 16 to 19 remain additional Region A requirements; they are not assessed here.

You are the specialist for the law of Region A (region). You assess a proposed data transfer against the instruments in your corpus: Region A Personal Information Regulation.

Other jurisdictions in this system: Region B. You cannot read their law. If a requirement of your law depends on what another jurisdiction's law says, add a peer_question naming that jurisdiction's registry code and set open_dependency on the requirement; the supervisor routes it. Ask only what the other law provides on a point your own requirement depends on; never ask another specialist to assess your requirement, or to assess or confirm another corpus's provisions.
Lower-level corpora you may delegate to: subregion_a1. Where your law leaves a matter to that law, delegate a specific question with the provisions that leave it open. The delegate also reports further requirements of its own law.

METHOD
1. Decide whether your law applies to any party or activity in the case, from its scope provisions.
2. Work through your table of contents and identify every requirement your law imposes that the facts engage, including definitions that change the analysis and cumulative conditions in other provisions.
3. Assess each requirement. Keep requirements for different actors or activities separate.
4. Delegate and raise peer questions where needed.
5. In coverage_note, say how you checked nothing engaged was missed and what remains limited.

RULES
- The laws in your corpora are the only law. Do not import rules from any real-world legal system; if your general knowledge suggests a rule the text does not contain, or contradicts the text, follow the text.
- Facts: refer to FACT PASSAGES by fact_id. Requester statements are claims; evidence summaries describe what each document says.
- Treat the stated facts and described arrangements as complete. If a requirement fails on them, mark it unmet "as described" and put the cure in required_actions. A supplied document that addresses a requirement establishes it; list elements it omits as confirmations, not as blockers.
- status: met | unmet | undetermined (a decisive fact, document or answer from other law is missing: say which in missing_facts, missing_evidence or open_dependency) | not_applicable.
- kind: gate if the transfer may not proceed until it is met; duty if it is an ongoing obligation that does not decide whether this transfer may proceed.
- routes: for each requirement with alternatives or exceptions in the law, list every plausible one with a status. Do not stop at the first route that works if it carries its own prerequisites; a route that fails does not close the others. Route statuses are defined in the schema; apply them literally. supported means in place now. available means it would work for the transfer as proposed once the parties make the changes in required_actions: these are the routes forward. ruled_out means the law excludes the transfer as proposed, with a reason from the text. unresolved is only for a missing fact, document or answer, never for something not yet done. The status must match your reasoning: if your reasoning says the law excludes the route, it is ruled_out; if it says a change would make it work, it is available.
- A requirement is an obligation the law imposes. Each alternative way to meet it (a recognition, a set of clauses, an exception, a derogation) is a route inside that requirement, never a requirement of its own: one route failing does not make an obligation unmet while another route remains.
- Report only requirements created by your own instruments. ## A-REG 2 Article 2 - Material scope
[A-REG 2#L1] 1. This Regulation applies to the processing of personal information wholly or partly by automated means, and to other processing of personal information which forms part of a filing system.
[A-REG 2#L2] 2. This Regulation does not apply to processing:
[A-REG 2#L3] (a) by a natural person in the course of a purely personal or household activity;
[A-REG 2#L4] (b) of information which does not relate to an identified or identifiable person, including information rendered anonymous in such a manner that no person can be identified by any means reasonably likely to be used by the custodian or by any other person.

## A-REG 3 Article 3 - Territorial scope
[A-REG 3#L1] 1. This Regulation applies to processing in the context of the activities of an establishment of a custodian or an agent in a Subregion, regardless of whether the processing itself takes place in Region A.
[A-REG 3#L2] 2. This Regulation also applies to processing by a custodian or agent not established in Region A where the processing relates to offering goods or services to persons in Region A or to monitoring their behaviour within Region A.

## A-REG 4 Article 4 - Definitions
[A-REG 4#L1] For the purposes of this Regulation:
[A-REG 4#L2] (1) 'personal information' means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person;
[A-REG 4#L3] (2) 'health information' means personal information about the physical or mental health of a person, including information revealed by the provision of health care to that person;
[A-REG 4#L4] (3) 'genetic information' means personal information relating to the inherited or acquired genetic characteristics of a person;
[A-REG 4#L5] (4) 'sensitive information' means health information, genetic information and biometric information processed for the purpose of uniquely identifying a person;
[A-REG 4#L6] (5) 'custodian' means the person or body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing;
[A-REG 4#L7] (6) 'agent' means a person or body which processes personal information on behalf of a custodian;
[A-REG 4#L8] (7) 'pseudonymised information' means personal information which can no longer be attributed to a specific person without the use of additional information kept separately under technical and organisational measures;
[A-REG 4#L9] (8) 'third territory' means any state or territory which is not a Subregion;
[A-REG 4#L10] (9) 'outward transfer' means making personal information available to a recipient in a third territory, whether by sending, storing or hosting it there, or by permitting it to be accessed from a third territory;
[A-REG 4#L11] (10) 'Subregion' means a subregion of Region A listed in Annex I;
[A-REG 4#L12] (11) 'Authority' means the supervisory authority designated by a Subregion under Article 21.

## A-REG 6 Article 6 - Lawful grounds
[A-REG 6#L1] 1. Processing is lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following grounds applies:
[A-REG 6#L2] (a) the person has consented to the processing for one or more specific purposes in accordance with Article 7;
[A-REG 6#L3] (b) the processing is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the person is a party, or for steps taken at the person's request before entering into a contract;
[A-REG 6#L4] (c) the processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation under Region A or Subregion law to which the custodian is subject;
[A-REG 6#L5] (d) the processing is necessary to protect the vital interests of the person or of another natural person;
[A-REG 6#L6] (e) the processing is necessary for the performance of a public function vested in the custodian by Region A or Subregion law;
[A-REG 6#L7] (f) the processing is necessary for the legitimate interests of the custodian or a third party, except where those interests are overridden by the interests or rights of the person.
[A-REG 6#L8] 2. Point (f) of paragraph 1 is not available to public bodies in the performance of their functions, and is not available for the processing of sensitive information.

## A-REG 7 Article 7 - Conditions for consent
[A-REG 7#L1] 1. Consent shall be given by a clear written or electronic statement, specific to each purpose, and may be withdrawn at any time as easily as it was given.
[A-REG 7#L2] 2. A person under the age of 16 may not consent on their own behalf; consent shall be given by a person with parental responsibility. Subregion law may set a lower age, which shall not be below 13.

## A-REG 8 Article 8 - Sensitive information
[A-REG 8#L1] 1. Processing of sensitive information is prohibited.
[A-REG 8#L2] 2. Paragraph 1 does not apply where:
[A-REG 8#L3] (a) the person has given explicit consent to the processing for one or more specified purposes, except where Subregion law provides that the prohibition may not be lifted by consent;
[A-REG 8#L4] (b) the processing is necessary to protect the vital interests of the person or of another natural person where the person is physically or legally incapable of giving consent;
[A-REG 8#L5] (c) the processing is necessary for the purposes of preventive medicine, medical diagnosis or the provision of health care or treatment, on the basis of Subregion law, and the information is processed by or under the responsibility of a professional subject to an obligation of professional secrecy under Subregion law;
[A-REG 8#L6] (d) the processing is necessary for reasons of public interest in the area of public health on the basis of Region A or Subregion law;
[A-REG 8#L7] (e) the processing is necessary for scientific research in accordance with Article 20.
[A-REG 8#L8] 3. Subregions may maintain or introduce further conditions, including limitations, with regard to the processing of health information or genetic information.

## A-REG 12 Article 12 - Impact assessment
[A-REG 12#L1] 1. Where processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights of persons, the custodian shall, before the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing.
[A-REG 12#L2] 2. An impact assessment is required in particular in the case of:
[A-REG 12#L3] (a) processing of the sensitive information of more than 5,000 persons;
[A-REG 12#L4] (b) systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale.
[A-REG 12#L5] 3. Each Authority may establish and publish a list of further kinds of processing for which an impact assessment is required in its Subregion.
[A-REG 12#L6] 4. The assessment shall contain at least a description of the processing, an assessment of its necessity, an assessment of the risks and the measures envisaged to address them.

## A-REG 16 Article 16 - General principle for outward transfers
[A-REG 16#L1] An outward transfer may take place only where the other provisions of this Regulation are complied with and the transfer is covered by Article 17, Article 18 or Article 19.

## A-REG 17 Article 17 - Recognised third territories
[A-REG 17#L1] 1. The Commission may recognise that a third territory, a specified sector within it, or recipients holding a specified certification in it, ensure an adequate level of protection.
[A-REG 17#L2] 2. Recognitions in force are listed in Annex II, together with any limits attached to them.
[A-REG 17#L3] 3. A transfer is covered by a recognition only within its stated limits. A recognition limited to certified recipients covers only a recipient whose certification is active at the time of the transfer and extends to the kind of information transferred.

## A-REG 18 Article 18 - Approved transfer clauses
[A-REG 18#L1] 1. In the absence of a recognition covering the transfer, an outward transfer may take place where the exporter and the recipient have executed the transfer clauses approved by the Commission.
[A-REG 18#L2] 2. Before relying on paragraph 1, the exporter shall assess whether the law and practice of the third territory applicable to the recipient, including any power of public authorities to require disclosure of or access to the information, would prevent the recipient from complying with the clauses, and shall adopt supplementary measures where necessary to ensure protection essentially equivalent to that within Region A.
[A-REG 18#L3] 3. Where effective supplementary measures cannot be adopted, the transfer shall not take place on the basis of this Article.

## A-REG 19 Article 19 - Derogations for specific situations
[A-REG 19#L1] 1. In the absence of a recognition under Article 17 or of approved transfer clauses under Article 18, an outward transfer may take place only on one of the following conditions:
[A-REG 19#L2] (a) the person has explicitly consented to the proposed transfer after having been informed of the possible risks of the transfer in the absence of a recognition and of appropriate safeguards;
[A-REG 19#L3] (b) the transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract between the person and the custodian;
[A-REG 19#L4] (c) the transfer is necessary to protect the vital interests of the person or of other persons, where the person is physically or legally incapable of giving consent;
[A-REG 19#L5] (d) the transfer is necessary for important reasons of public interest recognised in Region A law or in the law of the Subregion to which the custodian is subject.
[A-REG 19#L6] 2. Points (a) and (b) of paragraph 1 apply only to transfers which are occasional and do not form part of a repetitive, structural or continuing series of transfers.
[A-REG 19#L7] 3. Points (a) and (b) of paragraph 1 are not available to public bodies in the performance of their functions.

## A-REG 5 Article 5 - Principles
[A-REG 5#L1] 1. Personal information shall be:
[A-REG 5#L2] (a) processed lawfully, fairly and transparently;
[A-REG 5#L3] (b) collected for specified and explicit purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with them;
[A-REG 5#L4] (c) adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for those purposes; where a purpose can be achieved with pseudonymised information, identifiable information shall not be used for it;
[A-REG 5#L5] (d) accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date;
[A-REG 5#L6] (e) kept in identifiable form for no longer than is necessary for the purposes;
[A-REG 5#L7] (f) protected by appropriate technical and organisational security measures.
[A-REG 5#L8] 2. The custodian shall be responsible for, and able to demonstrate, compliance with paragraph 1.

output.impact: The Subregion A1 answers resolve the prior dependencies. A1 law confirms the healthcare basis and professional-secrecy conditions, confirms that no special hosting/storage or A1 impact-assessment requirements apply, and expressly excludes the Article 19(1)(a) consent derogation for genetic information. The outward-transfer requirement therefore changes from met to unmet as described; the sensitive-information and impact-assessment requirements are updated accordingly. The newly read A-REG 21, Annex I and A-REG 20 do not change the outcome: A1 is a listed Subregion, Article 21 makes the applicable A1 provisions operative, and the referral is not scientific research.

changed_requirements.title: Sensitive-information prohibition and exception
changed_requirements.reasoning: The report, ECG summary and referral letter contain health and genetic information and therefore sensitive information under Article 4. Article 8(1)'s prohibition is lifted on the healthcare route in Article 8(2)(c): the processing is necessary for diagnosis and treatment, and A1 law confirms that processing is lawful when carried out by or under the responsibility of a registered practitioner. The A1 answer also confirms that the registered practitioner owes professional secrecy and may disclose to a third party with the patient's consent. The signed consent identifies the information, recipient, purpose and transfer risks. The A1 restriction on consent for genetic information applies to insurance or employment processing, not this treatment referral. The separate Article 19 consent restriction affects the outward-transfer requirement, not whether the underlying healthcare processing satisfies Article 8.

changed_requirements.title: Impact assessment
changed_requirements.reasoning: Article 12 requires an assessment where processing is likely to result in high risk and specifically requires one for sensitive information of more than 5,000 persons or large-scale systematic monitoring. This is a one-person, one-off clinical referral and is not large-scale monitoring. A1 law confirms that its additional impact-assessment list applies only to hosting or storage of a patient record system by an agent outside A1 or matching health information with insurer-held information. Harrow keeps the referral in its own clinical record for its own care and is not an agent hosting Kestrel's record system; neither clinic is an insurer and no insurer matching is described. No impact assessment is therefore required on the supplied facts.

events.system:
You supervise a multi-jurisdiction assessment of a proposed data transfer. You can see every corpus in the system (manifests and tables of contents). Specialists, each limited to its own corpus, read the law and own their findings.

SYNTHESIS
You own the combined conclusion: whether the requirements of every corpus can be satisfied together. Each specialist owns its individual findings; you cannot change them.
- Read LAW BEHIND THE FINDINGS: the passages each specialist was shown from the provisions its findings and routes cite. It is the only law you may rely on; cite it by quote_ids. Do not import rules from any real-world legal system.
- Check each gate's status and routes against those passages. Then choose one route per engaged gate so that all of them work together: compare requirements and required actions of different corpora that concern the same actor, data or time, and check that taking one route does not defeat another. Record that combination in route_plan, and the outcome as the schema defines it.
- Conflicts: incompatible_law where the law of two corpora pulls apart (resolvable if some combination of routes satisfies both, and name it); disagreement where two findings contradict each other on the same point. Apparent conflicts with a compatible route are resolvable.
- Evidence: the same standard the specialists apply.
- Facts: refer to FACT PASSAGES by fact_id. Requester statements are claims; evidence summaries describe what each document says.
- Treat the stated facts and described arrangements as complete. If a requirement fails on them, mark it unmet "as described" and put the cure in required_actions. A supplied document that addresses a requirement establishes it; list elements it omits as confirmations, not as blockers.
- Blockers: a blocker names the gate it blocks (requirement_ref) and the decisive gap: a fact, document or answer without which that gate cannot be decided. If the gate already lists confirmations, say why confirming them later is not enough. Points already listed as confirmations, duties, and routes outside your route_plan (fallbacks you did not choose) are never blockers: put them in notes. The outcome is undetermined only when a blocker or a disagreement remains. A missing fact or document cannot be supplied by a specialist: do not ask for it.
FOLLOW-UPS (one bounded round; the next pass is final)
- Each follow-up must settle a named legal dependency or a specific error that could change a gate, a route in your route_plan, or the outcome. Nothing else: no wording, no duties that cannot change the decision, no general re-checks.
- routings: OPEN QUESTIONS are peer questions specialists could not answer from their own law. Route each to the corpus whose law answers it (a top-level corpus or a lower-level one), restating it narrowly.
- corrections: name the corpus, the requirement ids, the kind of error, the passages that show it (quote_ids), and exactly what to reconsider. You may say what a passage appears to provide; never tell a specialist what status to give. For a disagreement, set out both positions with their refs and send it to the owning specialist. COVERAGE WARNINGS (structural: provisions a specialist's own cited law points to that it never read) justify a missed_provision correction only when the unread provision could change a gate or a route.
- A requirement that is really one route of another requirement of the same corpus is a defect: ask its specialist to fold it in. Never ask to fold requirements of different corpora together.
